reference.source: Miller's Review of Orthopaedics / Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: A focal injury of the talar dome articular cartilage and underlying subchondral bone, frequently following an ankle sprain or fracture
Medial dome lesions tend to be deeper and posterior; lateral lesions are often shallower and trauma-related
Presents with persistent deep ankle pain, swelling, catching and giving way after an ankle injury that fails to settle
Plain radiographs are often normal, so MRI or CT is needed when symptoms persist
MRI assesses cartilage and bone oedema, while CT best defines bony fragment and cyst geometry
Stable lesions are treated non-operatively; unstable or displaced lesions and those with subchondral cysts are considered for surgery
Surgical options range from debridement and microfracture to osteochondral grafting depending on size and chronicity
reference.pathophysiology: Shear and compressive forces during an inversion ankle injury damage the talar dome cartilage and subchondral bone, sometimes with an element of impaired subchondral blood supply. Disruption of the osteochondral unit produces bone oedema, cyst formation and, if the fragment separates, an unstable lesion or loose body. Persistent altered joint mechanics cause pain and can progress to ankle osteoarthritis.
additionalInvestigations: MRI to evaluate cartilage, bone oedema and stability
CT to define bony fragment and cyst dimensions
Assessment of hindfoot alignment and ligamentous stability
redFlags: A displaced osteochondral fragment causing locking
Signs of septic arthritis in a painful swollen ankle
Progressive joint-space loss indicating established osteoarthritis
reference.prognosis: Small stable lesions often improve with non-operative care; larger, cystic or unstable lesions have more guarded outcomes, and surgical results decline with lesion size, chronicity and revision surgery.
pitfalls: Attributing persistent post-sprain ankle pain to soft tissue and never imaging beyond radiographs
Underestimating lesion size and cyst formation by relying on plain films
Ignoring hindfoot malalignment or instability that predisposes to failure
Offering repeat marrow-stimulation for large lesions better served by grafting
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: Non-operative management of stable lesions with a period of protected weight-bearing or immobilisation, activity modification and physiotherapy
Analgesia and rehabilitation to restore ankle range of motion and strength
Arthroscopic debridement with bone-marrow-stimulating microfracture for small unstable lesions, and retrograde drilling where cartilage overlies a subchondral cyst
Osteochondral autograft or allograft transplantation, autologous chondrocyte implantation or fragment fixation for larger, cystic or failed lesions
Correction of contributing hindfoot malalignment and lateral ligament instability
Surveillance for progression to ankle osteoarthritis, with referral to a foot and ankle surgeon for unstable or displaced lesions
